questions.stem: What makes a force conservative?
options: The work it does on an object between two points does not depend on the path taken
The work it does on an object is always converted into thermal energy along the way
The force on the object stays constant in size and direction wherever it is moved
The work it does on an object depends on the length of the path between two points
questions.explanation: For a conservative force such as gravity, the work done between two points depends only on the start and end positions, so energy can be stored as potential energy and fully recovered. Friction is non-conservative: its work depends on the path length and the energy is lost as heat.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-conservative force?
options: Air resistance on a falling leaf
Gravity on a falling leaf
Gravity on an orbiting satellite
The weight of a book on a shelf
questions.explanation: Air resistance always opposes motion, so the work it does depends on the path and the mechanical energy it removes becomes thermal energy. Gravity is conservative in every case: the work it does depends only on the change in height.

questions.stem: Under what condition is the total mechanical energy of an object conserved?
options: When the net force on it is constant
When only conservative forces do work on it
When no forces at all act on it
When it moves at a constant speed
questions.explanation: Mechanical energy (kinetic plus potential) is conserved when non-conservative forces such as friction and air resistance do no work, so only conservative forces like gravity transfer energy. A falling ball has a force acting on it, yet its mechanical energy is conserved if air resistance is negligible.

questions.stem: A sled slides from rest down a frictionless track to a point 15 m lower. Using g = 9.8 m s⁻², what is its speed at that point?
options: 12 m s⁻¹
294 m s⁻¹
147 m s⁻¹
17 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: With no friction, mechanical energy is conserved: mgΔh = ½mv², so v = √(2gΔh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 15) ≈ 17 m s⁻¹. The mass cancels. Forgetting the square root gives 294, and leaving out the 2 gives √147 ≈ 12 m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: A pendulum bob passes through its lowest point at 3.0 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 9.8 m s⁻², how high above its lowest point does it rise?
questions.explanation: The kinetic energy at the bottom becomes gravitational potential energy at the top: ½mv² = mgh, so h = v²/2g = 9.0/19.6 ≈ 0.46 m. Leaving out the 2 gives 0.92 m.

questions.stem: A 40 kg child on a toboggan starts from rest at the top of a slope 10 m high and reaches the bottom at 12 m s⁻¹. Using g = 9.8 m s⁻², how much mechanical energy is converted to other forms by friction?
questions.explanation: The loss in gravitational potential energy is mgh = 40 × 9.8 × 10 = 3920 J. The kinetic energy at the bottom is ½ × 40 × 12² = 2880 J. The difference, 3920 − 2880 = 1040 J, was transformed into thermal energy and sound by friction, a non-conservative force.

questions.stem: A crate pushed along a floor slows down and stops after the push is removed. Which describes the work done by friction on the crate?
options: It is zero, because friction acts perpendicular to the crate's motion
It is negative work that transforms kinetic energy into thermal energy
It is positive work that transforms kinetic energy into thermal energy
It is negative work that transforms potential energy into kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Friction acts opposite to the displacement, so θ = 180° in W = Fs cos θ and the work is negative. This removes kinetic energy from the crate and appears as thermal energy in the crate and floor. Only a force perpendicular to the motion, such as the normal force here, does zero work.

questions.stem: A rope pulls a cart 10 m along level ground with a 50 N force directed at 60° above the horizontal. How much work does the rope do on the cart?
questions.explanation: Only the component of force along the displacement does work: W = Fs cos θ = 50 × 10 × cos 60° = 250 J. Using the whole force gives 500 J, and using sin 60° gives 433 J.

questions.stem: A box slides 4.0 m across a level floor. How much work does the normal force do on the box during this motion?
options: Positive work, because the normal force pushes the box up
Negative work, because the normal force opposes the weight
Work equal to the weight multiplied by 4.0 m
Zero, because the force is perpendicular to the displacement
questions.explanation: In W = Fs cos θ the angle between the normal force and the horizontal displacement is 90°, and cos 90° = 0, so no work is done. A force does work only if it has a component along the displacement.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg trolley starts from rest. A constant net force of 8.0 N acts on it over 4.0 m. What is its final speed?
options: 8.0 m s⁻¹
5.7 m s⁻¹
32 m s⁻¹
4.0 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: The work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy: W = Fs = 8.0 × 4.0 = 32 J = ½ × 2.0 × v², so v = √32 ≈ 5.7 m s⁻¹. Giving 32 confuses the work in joules with the speed.

questions.stem: What is the kinetic energy of a 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹?
questions.explanation: KE = ½mv² = 0.5 × 1500 × 20² = 3.0 × 10⁵ J. Leaving out the ½ gives 6.0 × 10⁵ J, and forgetting to square the speed gives 1.5 × 10⁴ J.

questions.stem: A cyclist doubles her speed. By what factor does her kinetic energy change?
options: It becomes half as large
It becomes eight times as large
It becomes four times as large
It becomes twice as large
questions.explanation: KE = ½mv², so kinetic energy is proportional to the square of the speed. Doubling v multiplies KE by 2² = 4.

questions.stem: A 1000 kg car travelling at 15 m s⁻¹ brakes with a constant braking force of 5000 N. How far does it travel while stopping?
questions.explanation: The braking force does work equal to the loss of kinetic energy: Fs = ½mv², so s = (0.5 × 1000 × 15²)/5000 = 112 500/5000 = 22.5 m. Leaving out the ½ gives 45.0 m.

questions.stem: A force-displacement graph for a force pushing a trolley is a straight line from 0 N at 0 m to 20 N at 0.50 m. How much work does the force do over the 0.50 m?
questions.explanation: Work is the area under a force-displacement graph. Here it is a triangle: ½ × 0.50 × 20 = 5.0 J. Multiplying the final force by the full displacement gives 10 J, which assumes the force was 20 N the whole way.

questions.stem: A 60 kg student climbs a staircase that rises 15 m. Using g = 9.8 m s⁻², what is the increase in her gravitational potential energy?
options: 88 kJ
4.4 kJ
8.8 kJ
questions.explanation: ΔU = mgΔh = 60 × 9.8 × 15 = 8820 J ≈ 8.8 kJ. Leaving out g gives 900 J, and 4.4 kJ would follow from wrongly including a factor of ½ as in kinetic energy.

questions.stem: A 0.50 kg ball falls 2.0 m. Using g = 9.8 m s⁻², what work does gravity do on it, and what is the change in its gravitational potential energy?
options: Gravity does +9.8 J of work; ΔU = −9.8 J
Gravity does −9.8 J of work; ΔU = +9.8 J
Gravity does +9.8 J of work; ΔU = +9.8 J
Gravity does +1.0 J of work; ΔU = −1.0 J
questions.explanation: The weight (4.9 N) acts in the direction of the 2.0 m displacement, so it does +9.8 J of work. The potential energy falls by the same amount, so ΔU = −9.8 J, and the kinetic energy rises by 9.8 J if air resistance is negligible.

questions.stem: A worker lifts a 20 kg box 1.5 m straight up at constant velocity. Which statement about the work done is correct?
options: The worker does +294 J, gravity does −294 J, and the box's kinetic energy is unchanged
The worker does +294 J, gravity does +294 J, and the box gains 588 J of kinetic energy
The worker does no work, because the box moves at constant velocity the whole time
The worker does +294 J, gravity does no work, and the box gains 294 J of kinetic energy
questions.explanation: At constant velocity the worker's force equals the weight, so she does mgh = 20 × 9.8 × 1.5 = 294 J. Gravity acts opposite to the motion and does −294 J. The net work is zero, so ΔKE = 0; the worker's energy is stored as gravitational potential energy.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown straight up and caught again at the same height. Ignoring air resistance, which describes its energy transformations?
options: Kinetic energy stays constant on the way up, then turns into potential at the top
Kinetic to gravitational potential on the way up, then back to kinetic on the way down
Gravitational potential to kinetic on the way up, then back to potential on the way down
Kinetic to thermal on the way up, then thermal back to kinetic on the way down
questions.explanation: As the ball rises it slows, so its kinetic energy becomes gravitational potential energy, all of it at the top. On the way down the potential energy turns back into kinetic energy. With no air resistance, it returns at its launch speed.

questions.stem: A box is raised to a shelf 1.2 m high, once by lifting it straight up and once by sliding it up a frictionless ramp. How does the work done against gravity compare?
options: It is the same, because gravity is a conservative force
It is greater for the ramp, because the path is longer
It is smaller for the ramp, because less force is needed
It is greater for lifting, because the force is larger
questions.explanation: The work done against gravity is mgΔh and depends only on the change in height, because gravity is conservative. The ramp needs a smaller force over a longer distance, but the product, the work, is the same.

questions.stem: A ball dropped from 2.0 m rebounds to a height of 1.5 m. What fraction of its mechanical energy was transformed into other forms in the bounce?
questions.explanation: Gravitational potential energy is proportional to height, so the ball keeps 1.5/2.0 = 75% of its energy and 25% is transformed into thermal energy and sound. 75% is the fraction kept, not the fraction lost.

questions.stem: What is the momentum of a 0.16 kg cricket ball travelling at 25 m s⁻¹?
options: 50 kg m s⁻¹
156 kg m s⁻¹
2.0 kg m s⁻¹
4.0 kg m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: p = mv = 0.16 × 25 = 4.0 kg m s⁻¹, in the direction of the velocity. Momentum is a vector, unlike kinetic energy. The value 50 comes from ½mv², which is the kinetic energy in joules.

questions.stem: A 0.20 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m s⁻¹ and rebounds along the same line at 8.0 m s⁻¹. What is the size of its change in momentum?
options: 1.6 kg m s⁻¹
3.6 kg m s⁻¹
0.40 kg m s⁻¹
2.0 kg m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Taking the rebound direction as positive, Δp = m(v − u) = 0.20 × (8.0 − (−10)) = 3.6 kg m s⁻¹. Ignoring the reversal of direction gives only 0.20 × 2.0 = 0.40 kg m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: The 0.20 kg ball that hits a wall at 10 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 8.0 m s⁻¹ is in contact with the wall for 0.020 s. What average force does the wall exert on it?
questions.explanation: From Δp = F_net Δt, F = 3.6/0.020 = 180 N, directed away from the wall. Ignoring the change in direction gives Δp = 0.40 kg m s⁻¹ and only 20 N; multiplying instead of dividing gives 0.072 N.

questions.stem: Why does an airbag reduce the force on a passenger's head in a crash?
options: It increases the time taken to stop, so a smaller force gives the same change in momentum
It reduces the change in momentum, so a smaller force is needed to bring the head to rest
It increases the change in momentum, so the force is spread over a much larger area
It reduces the time taken to stop, so the head loses its momentum before the force builds
questions.explanation: The head's change in momentum is fixed by its mass and speed. Since Δp = FΔt, stretching out the stopping time reduces the average force. The airbag does not change Δp; it changes how long the change takes.

questions.stem: A constant net force of 200 N acts for 0.050 s on a 0.50 kg ball that is initially at rest. What speed does the ball reach?
options: 20 m s⁻¹
10 m s⁻¹
5.0 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: The impulse is FΔt = 200 × 0.050 = 10 kg m s⁻¹, which equals the change in momentum. So v = 10/0.50 = 20 m s⁻¹. Giving 10 stops at the impulse without dividing by the mass.

questions.stem: Under what condition is the total momentum of a system conserved?
options: When the collision is perfectly elastic
When no internal forces act between the objects
When the objects move at constant speed
When no net external force acts on the system
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved in an isolated system, one with no net external force. This holds for elastic and inelastic collisions alike; it is kinetic energy that is conserved only in elastic ones. The internal forces between colliding objects are what change their individual momenta.

questions.stem: Why is momentum conserved when two trolleys collide on a frictionless track?
options: By Newton's first law each trolley keeps its velocity during the collision, so momentum cannot change
Kinetic energy is always conserved in a collision, and momentum is calculated from kinetic energy
By Newton's third law the forces cancel on each trolley, so neither trolley's momentum changes
By Newton's third law they exert equal and opposite forces for the same time, so their impulses cancel
questions.explanation: Each trolley pushes on the other with an equal and opposite force for exactly the same contact time, so their impulses are equal and opposite. One gains exactly the momentum the other loses, so the total is unchanged. The forces act on different trolleys, so they do not cancel on either one.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. What is their common velocity just after the collision?
options: 2.0 m s⁻¹
3.0 m s⁻¹
1.5 m s⁻¹
6.0 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Total momentum before = 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 kg m s⁻¹. After, (2.0 + 1.0)v = 6.0, so v = 2.0 m s⁻¹. Giving 6.0 states the momentum rather than the velocity.

questions.stem: The 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0 m s⁻¹ sticks to the stationary 1.0 kg trolley, and they move off at 2.0 m s⁻¹. How should the collision be classified?
options: Elastic, because the momentum stays at 6.0 kg m s⁻¹ throughout
Inelastic, because the momentum falls from 9.0 to 6.0 kg m s⁻¹
Elastic, because the kinetic energy stays at 9.0 J throughout
Inelastic, because the kinetic energy falls from 9.0 J to 6.0 J
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy before = ½ × 2.0 × 3.0² = 9.0 J; after = ½ × 3.0 × 2.0² = 6.0 J. Kinetic energy was lost, so the collision is inelastic. Momentum is conserved in every collision with no external force, so it cannot be used to classify one.

questions.stem: A 1.0 kg puck at 4.0 m s⁻¹ strikes a stationary 3.0 kg puck. The 1.0 kg puck rebounds at 2.0 m s⁻¹ and the 3.0 kg puck moves off at 2.0 m s⁻¹. What kind of collision is this?
options: Elastic: total momentum is 4.0 kg m s⁻¹ before and 8.0 after
Elastic: total kinetic energy is 8.0 J both before and after
Inelastic: total kinetic energy falls from 8.0 J to 6.0 J
Inelastic: the lighter puck reverses and loses its momentum
questions.explanation: Momentum checks out: 4.0 before and −2.0 + 6.0 = 4.0 kg m s⁻¹ after. Kinetic energy before is ½ × 1.0 × 16 = 8.0 J; after it is 2.0 + 6.0 = 8.0 J. Since kinetic energy is conserved, the collision is elastic.

questions.stem: A moving ball collides head-on and elastically with an identical stationary ball. What happens immediately afterwards?
options: The first ball stops and the second moves off with the first ball's velocity
Both balls move off together at half the first ball's velocity
The first ball rebounds at its original speed and the second stays still
Both balls move off at the same speed in opposite directions
questions.explanation: Only this outcome conserves both momentum and kinetic energy for equal masses: the velocities are exchanged. Moving off together at half speed conserves momentum but halves the kinetic energy, so that would be a perfectly inelastic collision.

questions.stem: What distinguishes an elastic collision from an inelastic one?
options: Total kinetic energy increases in an elastic collision and decreases in an inelastic one
Total kinetic energy is conserved in an elastic collision but not in an inelastic one
Total momentum is conserved in an elastic collision but not in an inelastic one
The objects stick together in an elastic collision but separate in an inelastic one
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved in both kinds if no external force acts. In an elastic collision kinetic energy is also conserved; in an inelastic one some becomes thermal energy, sound or deformation. Objects that stick together have had a perfectly inelastic collision.

questions.stem: A 70 kg skater and a 50 kg skater stand still on smooth ice and push apart. The 70 kg skater moves off at 1.0 m s⁻¹. What is the velocity of the 50 kg skater?
options: 1.4 m s⁻¹ in the same direction
0.71 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction
1.0 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction
1.4 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction
questions.explanation: The total momentum starts at zero and stays zero: 70 × 1.0 = 50 × v, so v = 1.4 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. Inverting the mass ratio gives 0.71 m s⁻¹; the lighter skater must move faster, not slower.

questions.stem: A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 0.010 kg bullet at 400 m s⁻¹. What is the recoil speed of the rifle?
options: 4.0 m s⁻¹
1.0 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Momentum before firing is zero, so the rifle's momentum equals the bullet's in the opposite direction: 4.0v = 0.010 × 400 = 4.0, so v = 1.0 m s⁻¹. Giving 4.0 states the momentum, not the speed.

questions.stem: In the recoil of a rifle firing a bullet, what happens to the total momentum and total kinetic energy of the rifle and bullet?
options: Momentum stays zero, while kinetic energy increases from chemical energy
Momentum increases from zero, while kinetic energy stays the same
Momentum and kinetic energy both stay zero throughout
Momentum stays zero, while kinetic energy decreases to zero
questions.explanation: No external force acts along the barrel, so the total momentum stays zero: the two momenta are equal and opposite. Their kinetic energies are both positive, though, and do not cancel; this energy comes from the chemical energy of the propellant.

questions.stem: A 1200 kg car travelling east at 15 m s⁻¹ collides head-on with an 800 kg car travelling west at 10 m s⁻¹. The cars lock together. What is their velocity just after the collision?
options: 5.0 m s⁻¹ east
13 m s⁻¹ east
5.0 m s⁻¹ west
2.5 m s⁻¹ east
questions.explanation: With east positive, total momentum = 1200 × 15 − 800 × 10 = 10 000 kg m s⁻¹. Dividing by 2000 kg gives 5.0 m s⁻¹ east. Adding the two momenta as if both cars moved east gives 13 m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: In a school investigation of momentum in collisions, trolleys run on a track tilted very slightly downhill. Why?
options: To balance friction so the net external force is close to zero
To make the trolleys accelerate so that the collision is elastic
To increase the momentum so the measurements are more precise
To make sure the trolleys stick together when they collide
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved only if the net external force is zero. Tilting the track just enough that a trolley rolls at constant velocity lets the weight component balance friction, so the system behaves as if isolated.

questions.stem: In a collision investigation, the measured total momentum is 1.20 kg m s⁻¹ before and 1.12 kg m s⁻¹ after. What is the percentage difference, and the most likely cause?
options: 7.1%, from friction acting as an external force
7.1%, from kinetic energy lost in the collision
6.7%, from friction acting as an external force
6.7%, from kinetic energy lost in the collision
questions.explanation: The difference is 0.08/1.20 × 100 ≈ 6.7% of the initial momentum. Friction is an external force, so it changes the system's momentum. Kinetic energy lost in an inelastic collision does not change the total momentum, so it cannot explain the difference.
